story_text.value:
Between Slack, Claude, GPT, and Gmail, I'm constantly making formatting changes: deleting timestamps and Slack's (edited), making API fields inline code, removing weird highlighting, etc.

I tried changing this with prompts, but for things like formatting rules, it didn't get applied consistently.

So I built Exro. It scans the pasted text and applies deterministic changes with no grammar/copy changes whatsoever. You can paste something in and try it directly. Let me know if you have any suggestions!

story_text.value:
An experiment using Jev to generate landing pages in real time. Jev is great at picking between different options so I attempted to break down the langing page UI into a set of choices for the model to choose from.

How this works: 1. Users type what kind of page they want and Jev decides what each line is (headline, fact, assertion etc.) 2. Jev makes choices for each layer of the page (opening, stage, light, depth etc.). Parameterizing design is hard (impossible?) but this took some tuning with Claude 3. A full page is constructed with a single call of about 90 questions.

Of course using an LLM would be more prudent for step 1, but I wanted to check the limits of Jev's understanding (it works pretty well in my opinion!).

title.value: Show HN: Jev-pages – Building landing pages real time with Jev

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

Ever since I started skiing 2 years ago, I've been completely obsessed with skiing and all aspects of going on a ski trip (the scenery, the food, the thrill of skiing, the community).

I was looking at the different ski tracking apps out there but none of them met my need: simple, give me a big living map showing an overview of my ski journey, and let me track exact slopes I’ve ridden with stats like how many red and black runs I've done.

No other app does this, and that was my motivation to build Slopely.

This has been an absolutely beautiful project for me as I get to work on something I’m passionate about. I also get to work with map technology, which I find very fascinating. Map is quite a nice medium to build applications on. I built this app thankfully to a lot of open source/free map technologies like MapTiler, OpenSkiMap, OpenFreeMap, OpenStreetMap

If you're a fellow skier or snowboarder, please give it a try and let me know what you think.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm building skins.dev : Most AI tools help you build your own tool from scratch, but usually there's already a tool that gets you 80% there. Skins is for the other 20%: you describe what's missing in a web app you use, and we handle the rest, whatever it takes: from simple JS scripts and styles up to new backend features (hosted on our Cloudflare-compatible serverless cloud), so your feature can call other APIs and even have its own SQLite database.

How it works: go to the page you'd like to change and press "Record" in the extension. We use the DOM snapshots and network requests to build a replica environment where coding agents can iterate safely. The Chromium extension then injects the changes per site via chrome.userScripts (à la Tampermonkey).

I'm building a library of ready-made templates, inspired by long-open feature requests on SaaS forums (Salesforce, Jira, HubSpot): https://skins.dev/blog/

Currently Chromium only (we're working on getting the latest version into the Chrome Web Store). I would love feedback, and curious what you'd change first in a tool you use daily :)

story_text.value: I got recently laid off and wanted to learn and play with tools that are popular today as an exercise. Homebrew has some interesting analytics, but it only provides snapshots, you don't have a feel how the popularity of competing tools and technologies changed over time. So I started to take weekly snapshots of the last 30 days data of both formulas and casks. While I had some initial success with clustering packages based on their descriptions, but so far I wouldn't leave it on autopilot. However it serves as a reasonable basis for manual curation. I'd appreciate ideas on how to improve identifying packages of the same domain. (https://github.com/greg76/toth) One of the first surprises for me was that how Codex has been gaining momentum for the last two months compared to Claude Code. Also, while I was looking into the data rolling in, the drop of downloads across the board looked suspicious. I have reached out to the homebrew team and they confirmed that 7.0.0 introduced a regression in analytics reporting and with a sameday fix 7.0.6 should be reporting data as before.

title.value: Show HN: Top of the Hops – Homebrew trends and comparisons

story_text.value:
I built this app mainly for myself and my wife. We both work in consulting and have tons of meetings every week.
I had tried many of the existing meeting copilots but never found something that actually fulfilled what I wanted.
Mainly, I wanted to be able to see in real time what's being said, irrespective of the language being spoken, including when people switch languages mid-meeting, which happens a lot in my work. I also wanted it translated in real time into my language, and I wanted suggestions for what to say that are grounded in actual web search rather than just the model making something up.
I use Soniox for transcription and Exa.ai for web search.
Bearbits runs in the browser and doesn't join the meeting as a bot.
Looking forward to your feedback, especially on whether this kind of real-time assistance is useful to you or just distracting.

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

As an amateur astronomer living in New York City, finding objects in the night sky has always been a huge challenge. I thought about using the smartphone's gyroscope and magnetometer, but the accuracy left a lot to be desired.

Then I learned about plate solving: given a picture of the sky, we can determine exactly where in the sky the camera was pointing by identifying the star pattern. This was a much better fit - as long as the phone and the optics are rigidly connected, we can repeatedly photograph the sky and determine the pointing direction with very high accuracy.

A lot of work was done to design an algorithm that works reliably with smartphone cameras, which have limited light sensitivity and wider field of view which includes buildings and trees. I experimented a lot with machine learning, and to my surprise, traditional CV methods actually performed better at extracting stars from the image.

The result is AstroHelm, an iOS and Android app that helps figure out where your telescope or camera is pointing, and guides you to the object of your choice. Just follow an arrow on screen, and the object will land right in your eyepiece or viewfinder. Everything happens on device, and no internet connection is required.

AstroHelm is free to use and comes with beginner-friendly objects selected for each night. Optional one time purchases unlock more objects and advanced features, such as interoperability with other astronomy software. I am also proud to partner with astronomy clubs and organizations to offer free licenses for outreach.

I hope AstroHelm can make it a little easier to discover the wonders of the night sky, and I look forward to your feedback!

story_text.value:
We have built an authentication protocol enabling mid-session real-time identity verification between final users during any active communication, delivered via a proprietary decoupled channel.

System allows users to send identity verification challenges to each other on-demand during communication. The goal is to prevent identity takeover by real-time audio deepfakes.

It is inspired in 3DS credit card processing –taking away the UX nightmare; some similarities: decoupled rail for authentication, enrolment, user redirection to trusted authentication mechanism.

The method is based on cryptographic credential management, employing only open standards via a proprietary algorithm. The server relays messages and serves for message-hardening enforcement.

Cryptographic operations, source of truth and decisions are all on the client-side. The model could be considered P2P in essence and usability –despite the existence of a limited-role server as a minimal required infrastructure. Our servers do not process or store any PII.

Our first use case is applied to regular carrier mobile phone calls, and requires installing a mobile app to function. Also, the protocol can be applied and integrated into any communication.

It would be great if you’d like to have a look at it and let us know what you think. I will be here to discuss online.

You can download the app and test it (limited testers):

- Android link: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.mistis.aut...

- iOS app link: https://testflight.apple.com/join/Rb5sXpwp

Testing involves at least two users, as the method requires pairing (cryptographic credential exchange) previously to establishing a regular phone call in which to send identity verification challenges. I can volunteer for testing if you cannot find a peer tester.

If you spot a weird bug or would like to mention anything in private, please drop a line to support@mistis.tech.

Justin (Founder)
